1086.title: On tiptoe
1086.hook: on tiptoe you can't stand firm; striding, you won't go far (Tao Te Ching 24)
1086.howItsDone: Some people who read the Tao Te Ching use chapter twenty-four as a check on themselves: when they notice strain or showing off, they come back to a plain, steady way of standing and working.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the whirlwind: a violent wind can't last a whole morning, so say little. Your line was speak little. A new week starts here.

If you're standing, try this. If you're sitting, just imagine it. Rise up onto your toes, as high as you can. For a second you're taller. Then the calves start to burn, the ankles wobble, and your arms go out looking for balance. You can't stay there, and you can't walk well like that either. Come back down, and feel the whole foot take the floor again: heel, arch, toes. That's steadiness, and it cost nothing. Chapter twenty-four of the Tao Te Ching starts right there, with a person straining on their toes.
screen: `RISE ONTO YOUR TOES.` → `THE WOBBLE.` → `COME BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: First, tiptoe, not firm. In Legge's translation the chapter begins: "He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm." The extra height is borrowed, and it has to be paid back quickly. Second, striding, not far. The next line says the same of walking. Whoever stretches their legs into long strides won't get far. A person who lunges down the road wears out before someone who just walks. The chapter is about posture, but not only about feet. Third, chapter twenty-two, in reverse. Two days ago, chapter twenty-two said the sage doesn't display himself, and so he shines; doesn't boast, and so his work counts. Chapter twenty-four turns the same lines inside out. Whoever shows himself off isn't seen clearly. Whoever insists he's right doesn't stand out. Whoever boasts gets no credit. Whoever is proud of himself doesn't last. Showing off is a kind of standing on tiptoe: you look taller, and you can't hold it. Fourth, leftover food, a growth. Then a blunt image. To the Way, the chapter says, these straining habits are like leftover food, or a useless growth on the body, things people turn away from. So whoever has the Way doesn't stay in them. It isn't a moral scolding so much as a diagnosis: the strain is extra. It weighs on you and gets you nowhere.
screen: `TIPTOE, NOT FIRM.` · `STRIDING, NOT FAR.` · `CHAPTER TWENTY-TWO, IN REVERSE.` · `LEFTOVER FOOD, A GROWTH.` · then, large: `HE WHO STANDS ON HIS TIPTOES DOES NOT STAND FIRM.`

segments.voice: Sit with both feet flat on the floor, and feel them there. Bring to mind one place where you're up on your toes, trying to look like you have it handled or pushing faster than things can go. Don't solve it; let your weight come down into your feet, and ask what standing on the whole foot would look like there.
On tiptoe. Chapter twenty-four's picture of strain: taller for a moment, never firm, and a stride too long to last. Today's word.
Your line: flat feet. The extra height is borrowed; the whole foot costs nothing. See you tomorrow.

1087.title: Something before heaven
1087.hook: something formed before heaven and earth; the Tao follows what is so of itself (Tao Te Ching 25)
1087.howItsDone: In Taoist thought, ziran, being so of itself, is an ideal: some practitioners spend time in nature or in quiet watching to sense how things unfold without being forced.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was on tiptoe: taller for a moment, never firm. Your line was flat feet.

A plant on a kitchen windowsill. Nobody turned it. Nobody gave it instructions. But over a few weeks every leaf has swung around to face the glass, the stems leaning toward the light like people at a parade barrier. It didn't try. It didn't decide. It just did what a plant does. Chapter twenty-five of the Tao Te Ching reaches back before the world began, and then lands on something as ordinary as that plant: a thing being what it is.
screen: `A PLANT ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `NOBODY TURNED IT.` → `IT JUST DID WHAT IT DOES.`

segments.voice: First, something before heaven. In Legge's translation the chapter opens: "There was something undefined and complete, coming into existence before Heaven and Earth." Still, formless, standing alone, it says, not changing, going everywhere without wearing out. It could be called the mother of everything under heaven. Second, no name, so call it the Way. Then the speaker admits a problem. He doesn't know its name. So he calls it Tao, the Way, and if pushed for a name, he calls it great. And great, the chapter says, means it goes far out, and going far out, it comes back. Third, each takes its law from the next. Near the end comes a chain. People follow the earth. The earth follows heaven. Heaven follows the Way. You'd expect the chain to stop there, at the top. It doesn't. Fourth, the Way follows ziran. The last link, in Legge's words: "The law of the Tao is its being what it is." The Chinese word there is ziran. Translators render it as what is so of itself, or naturalness, or spontaneity. Not a higher power above the Way, but the Way simply being itself, the way the plant leans toward the window without being told. So the chapter climbs past heaven, and at the very top finds no ruler at all, only something doing what it does. Some readers take this as a key to the whole book: the deepest thing isn't forced, and doesn't force.
screen: `SOMETHING BEFORE HEAVEN.` · `NO NAME, SO CALL IT THE WAY.` · `EACH TAKES ITS LAW FROM THE NEXT.` · `THE WAY FOLLOWS ZIRAN.` · then, large: `ITS BEING WHAT IT IS.`

segments.voice: Find something alive nearby, a plant, a tree out the window, your own breath, and just watch it, without helping or judging. Notice how much is happening with no effort from you at all. If your mind starts to manage, let it rest and go back to watching.
Ziran. What is so of itself: naturalness, the way a thing is when nothing is pushing it. In chapter twenty-five, it's what even the Way follows. Today's word.
Your line: so of itself. At the top of the chain, nothing is pushing. Go gently.

1088.title: Heavy is the root
1088.hook: the heavy is the root of the light; stillness masters restlessness (Tao Te Ching 26)
1088.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-six as guidance for leaders and parents: staying calm and grounded when others are agitated, so that the steadiness, not the noise, sets the tone.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ziran, what is so of itself, the thing even the Way follows. Your line was so of itself.

There's a toy for small children, round at the bottom, sometimes painted with a face. Push it over and it rocks, wobbles, and comes back upright. Push it harder and it comes back anyway. The secret is a weight sitting low in its belly. The top can be as light and silly as you like, because the bottom is heavy. Some people are like that in a room. Voices rise, plans fall apart, someone slams a door, and that one person rocks a little and comes back to center. Chapter twenty-six of the Tao Te Ching is about where that weight comes from.
screen: `A TOY THAT WON'T STAY DOWN.` → `A WEIGHT DOWN LOW.` → `ONE PERSON IN A ROOM.`

segments.voice: First, the heavy roots the light. In Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "Gravity is the root of lightness; stillness, the ruler of movement." Gravity there means weight, seriousness, groundedness. The quick and changeable things need something heavy underneath them to grow from. Second, stillness rules restlessness. Stillness isn't only the root; it's the ruler. Movement and agitation come and go, but the still thing is the one in charge. It's easy to assume the loudest voice is running the room. The chapter says the steady one is. Third, never far from the baggage cart. Then an image from travel. The wise person, the chapter says, can march all day and never stray far from the heavy baggage wagon. Even with splendid sights all around, he stays calm and settled, and doesn't wander off after them. Fourth, light, and the root is lost. The chapter ends with a warning aimed at a ruler, someone with great power. How can such a person treat themselves lightly before the world? Act lightly, and you lose your root. Be restless, and you lose your rule. A person who grabs at every passing thing has cut loose from their own weight. This isn't a call to be heavy in the sense of gloomy. It's a call for a center of gravity, low and settled, so the rest of a life can move freely on top of it.
screen: `THE HEAVY ROOTS THE LIGHT.` · `STILLNESS RULES RESTLESSNESS.` · `NEVER FAR FROM THE BAGGAGE CART.` · `LIGHT, AND THE ROOT IS LOST.` · then, large: `GRAVITY IS THE ROOT OF LIGHTNESS.`

segments.voice: Sit and let yourself get heavy: body into the chair, feet into the floor, the breath dropping low like the weight in that toy. Then picture a room you'll be in today, a kitchen, a meeting, a car, with yourself in it, low and calm while things move around you. You don't have to fix anything; just be the one who comes back upright.
Heavy is the root. Chapter twenty-six's teaching that weight grounds what is light, and stillness rules what is restless. Today's word.
Your line: stillness masters. The loudest voice isn't the one running the room. Until tomorrow.

1089.title: No tracks
1089.hook: a good traveler leaves no tracks, and the sage rejects no one (Tao Te Ching 27)
1089.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching put chapter twenty-seven into practice through small unseen acts of care, tidying, repairing, helping, done without leaving any mark of who did them.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was heavy is the root: weight grounds the light, and stillness rules the restless. Your line was stillness masters.

Early morning at a lakeside campsite. The tent is down and rolled. The fire ring is cold, the stones put back where they were found. Someone has walked the whole site once, head down, picking up a bottle cap and a twist tie that weren't even theirs. By the time the car pulls away, the clearing looks the way it did before they came, maybe a little better. The next family will never know anyone was there. Hikers have a phrase for this: leave no trace. Chapter twenty-seven of the Tao Te Ching says something like it, in its own way.
screen: `A CAMPSITE AT DAWN.` → `STONES PUT BACK.` → `LEAVE NO TRACE.`

segments.voice: First, no tracks, no tallies. In Legge's translation, the chapter opens: "The skilful traveller leaves no traces of his wheels or footsteps." Then a list in the same key. A good speaker says nothing anyone can find fault with. A good counter needs no tally sticks. The skill is so complete you can't see the machinery. Second, locks without bolts. A good closer shuts a door with no bolt, and still it can't be opened. A good binder ties with no rope, and still it can't be undone. What holds things together here isn't hardware. It's something quieter, like trust, or care so thorough it doesn't need a padlock. Third, no one thrown away. Then the chapter turns to people. The sage, it says, is good at saving people, and so no one is cast away. Good at saving things, and so nothing is thrown out. The chapter gives this a name, which translators render in different ways; some hear in it a hidden light. Fourth, teacher and material. The chapter ends with a pairing that can surprise. The good person is the teacher of the one who isn't good. And the one who isn't good is the good person's material, what they have to work with. If you don't honor your teacher, and don't care for your material, the chapter says, then however clever you are, you are badly lost. Leaving no tracks isn't only about tidiness. It's about doing good so quietly that nobody is rejected, and nobody is left owing.
screen: `NO TRACKS, NO TALLIES.` · `LOCKS WITHOUT BOLTS.` · `NO ONE THROWN AWAY.` · `TEACHER AND MATERIAL.` · then, large: `NO TRACKS, AND NO ONE CAST AWAY.`

segments.voice: Think through the places you'll pass through today: a shared kitchen, a bus seat, a friend's couch. Pick one, and one small thing that would leave it better, a wiped counter, a straightened chair. Picture yourself walking away from it, with nobody thanking you and nothing to show.
No tracks. Chapter twenty-seven's skilled traveler, who leaves no trace, and its sage, who throws no one away. Today's word.
Your line: no tracks. The finest skill hides its own machinery. That's today, done.

1090.title: Be the valley
1090.hook: know the strong, keep to the soft, and be the valley of the world (Tao Te Ching 28)
1090.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching treat chapter twenty-eight as a way of carrying strength: knowing how to be forceful, and choosing receptiveness and humility instead.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was no tracks: the skilled traveler leaves no trace, and the sage throws no one away. Your line was no tracks.

From the top of a ridge, the whole landscape seems to be leaning one way. Streams run down. Paths wind down. Birds drop down into the trees below. Down there, at the bottom, is the valley, and everything ends up in it: the water, the soil, the green, the people who built the village along the river. The peak gets the view. The valley gets the life. Chapter twenty-eight of the Tao Te Ching asks a person to choose the valley on purpose, while knowing full well what it's like to stand on the peak.
screen: `FROM THE TOP OF A RIDGE.` → `EVERYTHING RUNS DOWN.` → `THE VALLEY GETS THE LIFE.`

segments.voice: First, know the strong, keep to the soft. The chapter opens with a pair. In the Chinese, the words are male and female. Know the male, it says, but keep to the female. Some readers hear in the pair the strong and the soft. The point is not to be ignorant of strength. You know exactly what it is. You just don't live from there. Second, the valley of the world. Do that, the chapter says, and you become the stream-bed of the world, the low channel everything runs into. Later it says the same with another word: the valley of the world. Low, open, receiving. As with the ridge and the valley a moment ago, the high place is admired, but the low place is where things gather. Third, back to infant, back to uncarved. Then the chapter reaches back. It says that whoever is the stream-bed of the world returns to being an infant, and whoever is the valley returns to the uncarved block. Those are two pictures you've already met: drifting like an infant, eight days ago, and the plain uncarved wood, nine days ago. Here the book ties them together. The soft way leads back to the beginning. Fourth, great carving doesn't cut. The chapter ends with the uncarved block split up into useful vessels, and the sage, put to use, becoming a leader of officials. And then a final line, which some translators render as: the great carver does not cut. The best shaping, in this picture, leaves the thing whole.
screen: `KNOW THE STRONG, KEEP THE SOFT.` · `THE VALLEY OF THE WORLD.` · `BACK TO INFANT, BACK TO UNCARVED.` · `GREAT CARVING DOESN'T CUT.` · then, large: `BE THE VALLEY.`

segments.voice: Let your shoulders drop, the way water runs downhill. Bring to mind one place where you could push, an argument, a deadline, a person who's slow, and picture the soft way instead: a lower voice, an open question, a moment of making room. You're not giving up your strength; you're choosing not to lead with it.
Be the valley. Chapter twenty-eight's picture of a person who knows strength and keeps to softness, low and open, where everything gathers. Today's word.
Your line: be the valley. The peak gets the view; the valley gets the life. See you tomorrow.

1091.title: The sacred vessel
1091.hook: the world is a sacred vessel; try to seize it and you ruin it (Tao Te Ching 29)
1091.howItsDone: Some readers of the Tao Te Ching take chapter twenty-nine as a caution against overreach: they work toward what they want while letting go of control over how it turns out.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was be the valley: know the strong, keep to the soft, and stay low where everything gathers. Your line was be the valley.

A little kid with a bubble wand on a summer porch. One long breath, and out floats a bubble the size of a melon, wobbling, shining, turning colors. The kid is thrilled. And then does the obvious thing: reaches out with both hands to catch it. Pop. A wet spot on the palms, and a stunned face. Try again. Pop. The only way to keep watching the bubble is to leave it alone. Chapter twenty-nine of the Tao Te Ching says the whole world is like that bubble, and it says so to people who want to run things.
screen: `A BUBBLE ON A PORCH.` → `TWO HANDS REACH.` → `POP.`

segments.voice: First, trying to take the world. The chapter starts with someone who wants to take hold of the world and do something with it, fix it, run it, improve it. The speaker says plainly: I see that it can't be done. Second, a sacred vessel. Then the reason. The world, the chapter says, is a sacred vessel, a spirit-like thing. It can't be acted upon that way. In Legge's translation: "He who would so win it destroys it; he who would hold it in his grasp loses it." Grab it and you break it. Clutch it and it slips away. A vessel is a container, a made thing. Call it sacred, and it becomes something you handle carefully, with both hands, never roughly. Third, some lead, some follow. Next comes a list of how things actually are. Some go ahead, and some follow behind. Some breathe out warm, and some breathe out cold. Some are strong, some are weak. Some are up, some are down. The world has its own rhythms, its own back and forth, and a grabbing hand can't flatten them into one straight line. Fourth, no excess, no extremes. So what does the sage do? The chapter's answer is short: the sage lets go of the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive. Not nothing. Not passivity. Just no overreach. Like the kid on the porch, learning, bubble after bubble, that the best way to keep the shining thing is to stand back and breathe.
screen: `TRYING TO TAKE THE WORLD.` · `A SACRED VESSEL.` · `SOME LEAD, SOME FOLLOW.` · `NO EXCESS, NO EXTREMES.` · then, large: `HOLD IT IN YOUR GRASP, AND LOSE IT.`

segments.voice: Open your hands on your lap, palms up. Bring to mind one thing you're trying hard to make happen, and feel where your mind is gripping it. Without giving up on it, loosen the grip the way your hands are open now, and let it float like that bubble: still wanted, no longer squeezed.
The sacred vessel. Chapter twenty-nine's name for the world: a spirit-like thing that breaks when grabbed and slips away when clutched. Today's word.
Your line: don't grab it. The world is a thing for careful hands. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1092.title: Where armies camp
1092.hook: where armies camp, thorns grow; don't use force (Tao Te Ching 30)
1092.howItsDone: Readers of the Tao Te Ching often take chapter thirty as advice for anyone near power: do what is necessary, stop there, and remember that force leaves damage behind it.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was the sacred vessel: a world you ruin by trying to seize it. Your line was don't grab it.

A field after the soldiers have gone. The tents are packed, the fires are cold, the ground is trampled flat. Nobody plowed this season. Nobody had the chance. When something finally comes up, it isn't wheat. It's brambles. Chapter thirty of the Tao Te Ching takes that field and hands it to anyone who stands next to power. It also closes a week of chapters about not straining: standing on tiptoe, the heavy root, the valley, the vessel you can't seize. Today the same idea meets force head on.
screen: `A FIELD AFTER THE SOLDIERS LEAVE.` → `BRAMBLES, NOT WHEAT.` → `THE SAME IDEA MEETS FORCE.`

segments.voice: First, who the chapter is talking to. In James Legge's translation, it begins with someone who would assist a ruler in harmony with the Tao, and says that person won't assert mastery by force of arms. It isn't advice for the king. It's advice for the one at the king's elbow. Second, the reason, and the picture. Force, the chapter says, comes back around on the one who uses it. Then: "Wherever a host is stationed, briars and thorns spring up." A host is an army. Where it camps, the fields go untended, and what grows is what nobody wanted. Bad years, the chapter adds, follow in the wake of great armies. Force wins the day and sends its bill later. Third, the chapter doesn't say never act. It describes a capable leader who strikes when it's truly necessary, gets the result, and stops. No boasting, no pride, no pushing on to prove a point. And it warns that whatever is driven to the peak of its strength starts to grow old, and that isn't the way of the Tao. Fourth, closer to home. There's no army in the kitchen. But there are small campaigns: winning the fight about the thermostat, steamrolling a meeting, getting a kid to comply by sheer volume. Each one can work. The chapter's question is what grows on that ground afterward. A grudge. A silence. Someone who stops telling you things.
screen: `ADVICE FOR THE ONE AT THE KING'S ELBOW.` · `WHERE AN ARMY CAMPS, THORNS.` · `GET THE RESULT, AND STOP.` · `SMALL CAMPAIGNS AT HOME.` · then, large: `BRIARS AND THORNS SPRING UP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one quarrel that's still live, at home, at work, with a neighbor, and notice where you've been pushing. Then ask: what is the smallest thing that actually needs to happen here? Not winning, just that one thing; hold it, and let the rest of the campaign go quiet.
Where armies camp. Chapter thirty's picture: wherever an army is stationed, briars and thorns spring up. Force wins now and leaves the thorns for later. Today's word.
Your line: no force. The result is enough; the victory lap grows thorns. That's the week.
